nodes_source.source_quote: In this work, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method to explore the potential of traffic video data in improving the efficiency of ramp metering.
nodes_source.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and reformed as position matrices. The preprocessed video data serves as inputs for learning optimal control strategies directly from high-dimensional inputs.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Data available from corresponding author upon request, no public link provided.

nodes_source.source_quote: The simulation parameters regarding driving behaviors are calibrated based on empirical data.
nodes_source.description: Data used for calibrating simulation parameters related to driving behaviors in the SUMO microscopic traffic simulator.
nodes_source.reproducibility_rationale: Data used to support the results is available from corresponding author upon request, no public link provided.

nodes_process.source_quote: Vehicle locations are extracted from the traffic video frames and are reformed as position matrices.
nodes_process.description: Vehicle locations are extracted from raw traffic video frames and converted into position matrices.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, no specific tools or parameters named beyond the generic method.

nodes_process.source_quote: Since one matrix is insufficient to describe vehicle dynamics, we stack the matrices of consecutive N time steps to represent the state s_t: S_t = {m_t-(N-1),..., m_t}. For computation efficiency, down-sampling is introduced before the matrix stack to reduce the input dimensions and maintain sufficient information about vehicle positions.
nodes_process.description: Consecutive vehicle position matrices are stacked to form a comprehensive state representation. Down-sampling is applied to these stacked matrices to reduce their dimensionality, while preserving essential information for computational efficiency.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, explicit output dimensions provided for state matrix (implying 'N' and downsampled resolution), but generic tools.

nodes_process.source_quote: We adopt a deep neural network termed Q-network to approximate Q*(s,a). The neural network contains several convolutional layers and fully connected layers. The Q-network in Mnih et al. [30] is revised as Figure 7, which consists of three convolutional neural network (CNN) layers and one full connection (FC) layer for each output layer. Initialize the action-value function Q with random weights w.
nodes_process.description: A deep Q-network, a revised architecture based on Mnih et al. [30], is initialized with random weights. This network comprises three convolutional layers and one fully connected layer, designed to approximate the Q-function and predict speed/queue length.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, detailed architecture from Figure 7, most parameters stated, generic tools.

nodes_process.source_quote: The RL method aims at training the agent (Ramp meter) to find an optimal policy π* that maximizes the discounted cumulative reward G_t after time step t. The gradient-based algorithm Adam [28] is used to update w_i to minimize the loss function. The experience replay [30] stores the data prepared for training into the replay buffer... The target network [29] is introduced for a stable estimation of target value Q*(s,a). A multitask learning strategy is implemented... The ramp meter takes new action with the e-greedy strategy.
nodes_process.description: The Q-network is trained using deep Q-learning, which employs the Adam optimizer, experience replay, a target network, and a multitask learning strategy for simultaneous Q-value, speed, and queue length prediction. An epsilon-greedy strategy is used for action selection.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all required tools referenced or named, all parameters from Table 1 and text stated, and random seeds mentioned.

nodes_process.source_quote: The proposed method is evaluated in SUMO, an open-source microscopic traffic simulator [31]. The simulation is performed in the freeway connecting Qingdao and Huangdao through a tunnel in Shandong, China, as shown in Figure 5. The speed limits in the mainline and at the on-ramp are 80 and 40 km/h, respectively. The simulation parameters regarding driving behaviors are calibrated based on empirical data. The simulation time is 7:50 a.m. to 9:00 a.m.
nodes_process.description: A microscopic traffic simulation environment is configured using SUMO to model a specific freeway section (Qingdao-Huangdao, China). Road network geometry, speed limits, and calibrated driving behaviors based on empirical data are defined for the simulation period.
parameters_mentioned: speed limits in the mainline=80 km/h
speed limits at the on-ramp=40 km/h
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, specific tool (SUMO) named, all major setup parameters stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: A series of simulation experiments based on real-world traffic data are conducted to evaluate the proposed approach. The Q-network is trained in 10^6 training frames, and each scenario is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments.
nodes_process.description: The trained DRL model is evaluated by conducting 20 simulation experiments within the SUMO environment. Performance metrics, including mainline travel times, on-ramp queue lengths, and downstream traffic flows, are measured.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all experiment parameters stated, generic evaluation assumed.

nodes_process.source_quote: The second scenario adopts the PI-ALINEA method. The PI-ALINEA method fixes the length of the green phase and determines the length of the red phase in the current signal cycle based on the length of the red phase in the previous cycle and the downstream occupancies in the previous and current cycles. ô refers to the desired value for mainline occupancy, which is set to 16% in this study. KR = 90 and Kp = 50 are two regulator parameters in PI-ALINEA.
nodes_process.description: The PI-ALINEA ramp metering method, used as a baseline, is implemented and evaluated in the SUMO simulation environment. This method determines green and red phase lengths based on downstream occupancy and regulator parameters.
parameters_mentioned: desired value for mainline occupancy ô=16%
green time for each cycle is fixed with time step size L=4 s
red time for each cycle is given by rkL
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, specific tool (SUMO) named, all PI-ALINEA parameters and experiment details stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: The first scenario does not apply ramp metering.
nodes_process.description: A baseline scenario without any ramp metering control is simulated and evaluated within the SUMO environment to provide a reference for performance comparison.
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, specific tool (SUMO) named, all experiment parameters stated.

nodes_process.source_quote: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of information contained in video data. The control area is divided into eight subareas. The information in the subarea is removed from original data to generate perturbed data for each subarea. The impact of missing information for each subarea is evaluated in 20 simulation experiments with perturbed data.
nodes_process.description: A perturbation analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of missing video data. The control area is divided into eight subareas, and information from each subarea is systematically removed from the input data. The DRL method's performance is then re-evaluated using this perturbed data.
parameters_mentioned: control area is divided into eight subareas
evaluated in 20 simulation experiments with perturbed data
nodes_process.reproducibility_rationale: clarity=4, all experiment parameters stated, generic perturbation and evaluation.
